Introduction to Environmental Science: Environmental science
Interdisciplinary study of how humans interact with the environment
Sustainability
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations
Ecological footprint
The land and resources needed to support a lifestyle
Renewable resource
A resource that replenishes on a human timescale
Nonrenewable resource
A resource that cannot be replaced once used
Tragedy of the commons
Shared resources being depleted by individual self-interest
Anthropocentric view
Valuing the environment primarily for human benefit
Precautionary principle
Acting to prevent harm even without complete proof
Environmental justice
Fair distribution of environmental burdens across communities
Carrying capacity
The maximum population an environment can sustain indefinitely
Ecosystems and Energy Flow: A community of organisms together with their physical environment
An organism making its own food, usually by photosynthesis
An organism breaking down dead material and recycling nutrients
A feeding position in a food chain
About a tenth of energy passes to the next trophic level
The interconnected network of feeding relationships
Energy left after producers meet their own respiration needs
A large region defined by its climate and characteristic life
The role and resource use of a species in its ecosystem
Biodiversity and Conservation: Biodiversity
The variety of life at genetic, species, and ecosystem levels
Genetic diversity
Variation in genes within a population
Endemic species
A species found naturally in only one place
Keystone species
A species whose loss dramatically restructures its community
Indicator species
A species whose health signals broader ecosystem condition
Invasive species
A non-native species spreading and causing harm
Habitat fragmentation
Breaking continuous habitat into isolated patches
Endangered species
A species at serious risk of extinction
Ecosystem services
Benefits people receive from functioning ecosystems
Conservation biology
The science of protecting and restoring biodiversity
Ex situ conservation
Protecting species outside their natural habitat, as in seed banks
Human Population Dynamics: Demography
The statistical study of human populations
Birth rate
Births per thousand people per year
Total fertility rate
The average number of children per woman
Replacement fertility
The birth rate that keeps a population stable, near 2.1
Age structure diagram
A population pyramid showing distribution by age and sex
Demographic transition
The shift from high birth and death rates to low ones as economies develop
Doubling time
Years for a population to double at its current growth rate
Infant mortality rate
Deaths of infants per thousand live births
Population momentum
Continued growth after fertility falls, due to a young age structure
Urbanization
The growing share of people living in cities
Soil and Agriculture: A distinct layer within a soil profile
The nutrient-rich upper layer where most roots grow
Loss of soil to wind or water, often accelerated by farming
Alternating crops to maintain soil fertility and disrupt pests
Growing a single crop over a large area, raising pest vulnerability
Mid-century technologies that sharply raised crop yields
Combining methods to control pests with minimal pesticide
Pests evolving to survive chemicals meant to kill them
Salt accumulation in soil from repeated irrigation
Farming that maintains soil and resources long-term
Intensive livestock production with concentrated waste
Water Resources and Pollution: Watershed
The land area draining into a particular body of water
Aquifer
An underground layer of rock holding groundwater
Water table
The upper boundary of groundwater saturation
Point source pollution
Contamination from a single identifiable location
Nonpoint source pollution
Contamination from diffuse sources such as runoff
Eutrophication
Nutrient overload triggering algal blooms and oxygen loss
Dead zone
An oxygen-depleted area where most aquatic life cannot survive
Biological oxygen demand
Oxygen consumed by decomposition, indicating organic pollution
Desalination
Removing salt from seawater to make it drinkable
Wastewater treatment
Removing contaminants before returning water to the environment
Thermal pollution
Heated discharge lowering the oxygen capacity of water
Air Pollution and the Atmosphere: The lowest atmospheric layer, where weather occurs
The layer above the troposphere containing the ozone layer
A pollutant released directly into the air
A pollutant formed by reactions in the atmosphere
Haze formed when sunlight reacts with vehicle emissions
Precipitation acidified by sulfur and nitrogen oxides
Warm air trapping pollutants near the ground
Thinning of the protective stratospheric ozone layer
Treaty that successfully phased out ozone-depleting chemicals
Fine airborne solids that penetrate deep into the lungs
US law regulating emissions of major air pollutants
Energy Resources: Fossil fuel
Coal, oil, or natural gas formed from ancient organic matter
Coal
The most abundant but most carbon-intensive fossil fuel
Natural gas
The cleanest-burning fossil fuel, mainly methane
Hydraulic fracturing
Injecting fluid to release gas and oil from shale
Peak oil
The point of maximum extraction, after which output declines
Energy efficiency
Getting more useful work from the same energy input
Nuclear fission energy
Power generated by splitting heavy atomic nuclei
Nuclear waste
Long-lived radioactive material requiring secure storage
Cogeneration
Capturing waste heat from power generation for useful work
Energy return on investment
Energy obtained compared to energy spent obtaining it
Renewable Energy: Technology converting sunlight directly into electricity
Building design capturing sunlight without mechanical systems
Electricity generated by turbines driven by moving air
Power drawn from heat stored beneath the earth's surface
Energy released by burning organic material
Liquid fuel such as ethanol produced from crops
The challenge that wind and solar output varies with conditions
Technology such as batteries smoothing variable supply
Crediting customers for electricity they send back to the grid
Balancing emissions released against emissions removed
Waste Management: An engineered disposal site lined to protect groundwater
Contaminated liquid draining through buried waste
Burning waste to reduce volume, sometimes generating power
Reprocessing used materials into new products
Decomposing organic waste into usable soil amendment
Preventing waste before it is created, the most effective strategy
Discarded electronics containing valuable and toxic materials
Waste that is toxic, corrosive, flammable, or reactive
US program funding cleanup of contaminated sites
Evaluating environmental impact across a product's entire life
Climate Change: Greenhouse effect
Atmospheric gases trapping heat and warming the planet
Greenhouse gas
A gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that traps infrared radiation
Carbon dioxide
The most significant human-produced greenhouse gas by volume
Methane
A greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide per molecule
Global warming potential
A measure comparing a gas's warming effect to carbon dioxide
Carbon sink
A reservoir such as a forest or ocean absorbing carbon
Albedo
The reflectivity of a surface, affecting how much heat is absorbed
Positive feedback loop in climate
Warming that triggers further warming, such as ice melt
Ocean acidification
Falling ocean pH as seawater absorbs carbon dioxide
Sea level rise
Rising oceans from thermal expansion and melting ice
Paris Agreement
International accord committing nations to emissions targets
Climate adaptation
Adjusting systems to cope with changes already underway
Environmental Policy and Sustainability: Environmental Protection Agency
The US agency enforcing environmental regulations
National Environmental Policy Act
Law requiring environmental review of major federal actions
Environmental impact statement
A required analysis of a project's likely environmental effects
Endangered Species Act
US law protecting listed species and their habitat
Cap and trade
A system capping total emissions and letting firms trade allowances
Carbon tax
A fee charged per unit of carbon emitted
Command and control regulation
Rules setting specific limits and technologies
Cost-benefit analysis
Weighing the economic costs of a policy against its benefits
Externality
A cost or benefit falling on someone outside the transaction
Green building
Construction designed to minimise resource use and impact
Circular economy
An economy designed to reuse materials rather than discard them
